lessons.title: History and Global Industry of Crocodile Farming
lessons.body: Crocodile farming started in the 1960s in countries like Zimbabwe and South Africa, mainly to produce high-quality skins for luxury goods. Before farming, wild crocodiles were hunted almost to extinction. Today, legal farming supplies most crocodile skins worldwide. Global production is around 1.5 million skins per year, with major farms in Africa (Zimbabwe, South Africa, Zambia, Kenya), Asia (Thailand, Indonesia), and Australia. Africa produces about 30% of the world's crocodile skins, mostly Nile crocodile. The industry is worth over $500 million annually. In Africa, countries like Zimbabwe have around 50 farms, and South Africa has over 60. A single high-quality belly skin can sell for $300 to $800. Meat is also sold locally and exported. By-products like teeth, claws, and bones are used for jewelry and traditional medicine. Farming reduces pressure on wild populations and provides rural jobs. For a new farmer, the key is to understand that this is a long-term business: crocodiles take 3 to 5 years to reach market size. Start small with 20 to 50 hatchlings, and learn as you grow. Contact your national wildlife authority for permits before you buy any animal.

lessons.title: Species Selection: Saltwater, Nile, and Other Crocodilians
lessons.body: The two main species farmed in Africa are the Nile crocodile (Crocodylus niloticus) and the saltwater crocodile (Crocodylus porosus). Nile crocodiles are native to most of sub-Saharan Africa and are well-suited to warm climates. They grow to 4-5 meters, but farmed ones are usually harvested at 1.5-2 meters. Saltwater crocodiles are bigger and more aggressive, and they need brackish water. They are farmed in Australia and Southeast Asia, but in Africa, Nile crocodile is the best choice. Other species like the African slender-snouted crocodile and dwarf crocodile are not commercially farmed because they grow slowly and have less valuable skins. When choosing stock, buy from a registered farm or licensed breeder. Never take eggs or animals from the wild without a permit. A good Nile crocodile hatchling costs $20 to $50. You need a ratio of one male to three females for breeding. Check that the animals are healthy: clear eyes, no wounds, and active. Ask for records of parentage to avoid inbreeding. In Africa, Nile crocodile farms are common in Zimbabwe, South Africa, Zambia, and Kenya. If you are in West Africa, the Nile crocodile is still the best option. Avoid mixing species in the same pen, as they can fight and interbreed. Start with at least 10 females and 3 males if you plan to breed.

lessons.title: Legal and CITES Regulations for Crocodile Farming
lessons.body: Crocodile farming is heavily regulated because all crocodile species are listed under CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species). Nile crocodile is in Appendix I or II depending on the country. In most African countries, you need a permit from the national wildlife authority, such as Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authority, South African National Parks, or Kenya Wildlife Service. To start a farm, you must apply for a captive breeding permit, which requires an approved facility, quarantine area, and a management plan. You also need CITES permits for any export or import of live crocodiles, skins, or meat. Each shipment must have a CITES export permit from your country and an import permit from the destination country. The permits cost $100 to $500 per shipment. You must tag each skin with a CITES non-detriment finding tag. Illegal trade carries heavy fines and prison. In Africa, many farms are involved in the CITES registered captive breeding program, which allows legal trade. Keep detailed records of births, deaths, and sales. Invite wildlife officers for inspections. It is also important to follow local animal welfare laws. Without proper permits, your products cannot be sold internationally. Work with a lawyer or consultant who knows wildlife law. The process can take 6 to 12 months, so start early.

lessons.title: Market Overview: Skins, Meat, and By-Products
lessons.body: The main product from crocodile farming is the skin, especially the belly skin. High-quality skins are used for luxury handbags, shoes, belts, and watch straps. The price depends on size, pattern, and quality. A 1.5-meter Nile crocodile belly skin can sell for $300 to $800. Classic belly skins with large scales are most valuable. Meat is the second product. Crocodile meat is white, low in fat, and high in protein. It sells for $10 to $20 per kilogram in local markets and up to $30 per kilogram in export markets. In Africa, restaurants in tourist areas and cities buy crocodile meat. By-products include teeth, claws, bones, and skulls, which are sold as curios, jewelry, or traditional medicine. A set of teeth can fetch $20 to $50. The global crocodile skin market is dominated by luxury brands like HermÃ¨s and Louis Vuitton. Africa exports about 300,000 skins per year. The main markets are Europe, Asia, and the USA. To succeed, you need to produce consistent quality. Skins must be properly salted or chrome-tanned. Many African farmers sell raw skins to tanneries in South Africa or Zimbabwe. You can also sell directly to international buyers if you have CITES permits. Meat is often sold locally to avoid export regulations. Start by contacting local tanneries and restaurants to understand demand. Join a farmer association to get better prices.

lessons.title: Basic Biology and Behavior of Crocodiles
lessons.body: Crocodiles are reptiles, so they are cold-blooded. They cannot control their body temperature internally. They need to bask in the sun to warm up and shade or water to cool down. Their ideal body temperature is 30-33Â°C. If it gets too cold, they stop eating and grow slowly. If too hot, they can die. In Africa, you need a climate where temperatures stay above 20Â°C most of the year. Crocodiles are carnivores. In the wild, they eat fish, birds, and mammals. On a farm, you feed them chopped fish, chicken, and red meat. They eat 5-10% of their body weight per week. They have strong jaws and sharp teeth. They swallow food in chunks. They can go weeks without food but will fight if hungry. Crocodiles are territorial and aggressive, especially males. They need space. A grow-out pen should allow at least 1 square meter per crocodile. They are also cannibalistic; smaller ones can be eaten by larger ones. So you must sort by size. Breeding happens once a year. Females lay 30-60 eggs in a nest. Incubation is 80-90 days at 28-32Â°C. The temperature determines the sex: lower temperatures produce females, higher produce males. Hatchlings are 25-30 cm long. They grow about 30 cm per year. They can live 50-70 years. Handle them with care using a noose pole and secure their jaws with tape.

lessons.title: Site Selection and Climate Requirements
lessons.body: Choosing the right site is critical. You need a location with a warm climate, plenty of water, and good security. Crocodiles need temperatures between 25Â°C and 35Â°C. In Africa, this means lowveld areas like the Zambezi Valley, Limpopo, or coastal regions. Avoid highlands where it gets cold. You need a reliable water source, such as a borehole, river, or municipal supply. Water quality must be good: pH 6.5-8.5, low chlorine. You will need to change water regularly. The site should be away from residential areas to avoid conflicts and smell. At least 500 meters from homes and 1 km from schools. The soil should be well-drained, like sandy loam, to prevent muddy pens. You need a slope of 1-2% for drainage. Security is vital: crocodiles can escape and hurt people. Use strong fences: 2-meter high chain-link with a concrete base. Add a double gate. You also need a building for incubating eggs and a quarantine area. Power supply for pumps and heaters is helpful. Roads must be accessible for feed and skin transport. Land size: for 100 crocodiles, you need about 0.5 hectares including pens, buildings, and buffer. Start with a small pen of 10m x 5m for 50 hatchlings. Get a topographic map and soil test. Consult local wildlife authority for site approval. Budget $5,000 to $10,000 for basic infrastructure.

quiz.q: In which decade did crocodile farming begin in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Crocodile farming started in the 1960s in countries like Zimbabwe and South Africa.

quiz.q: What is the most valuable product from crocodile farming?
